title: Vrika's boon
hook: an asura wins a deadly power by fierce austerity, and tries it on the god who gave it
tomorrow: a king of heaven becomes a snake

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shuka's clear sight. The self is pure; practice clears the mind. Book three, done.
screen: `THE SELF IS PURE; PRACTICE CLEARS THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Book four of the Yoga Sutras, the last, opens with where powers come from, and the Bhagavata Purana has a story that makes its point. An asura named Vrika asks the sage Narada: which god is quickest to please? Shiva, says Narada. He gives fast, and he angers fast. So Vrika goes to Kedara, builds a fire, and starts cutting pieces of his own flesh and offering them in. Day after day. At last he raises the blade to his own head, and Shiva rises out of the fire and stops his hand. Ask, says Shiva.
screen: `WHICH GOD IS QUICKEST TO PLEASE?` → `A FIRE AT KEDARA.` → `ASK, SAYS SHIVA.`

segments.voice: Vrika asks: let whoever's head I touch, die. Shiva grants it, and Vrika reaches straight for Shiva's head. Shiva runs, to the ends of the earth, with Vrika chasing, until Vishnu steps in, disguised as a young student. Politely he asks: you trust that boon? Test it first. On yourself. Vrika touches his own head, and falls. The story is half a joke and all a warning. Sutra 4.1: powers are born of birth, herbs, mantra, discipline or samadhi. Five sources, and only one is samadhi. Tapas, fierce discipline, works for an asura too, so a power proves nothing about the person holding it. The Gita says it more sharply. Austerities that are terrible and self-torturing, done out of ego, craving and force, it calls asuric, demonic. Then it gives the real measure of a holy person, the divine qualities, daivi sampat: fearlessness, purity of heart, generosity, self-control, truthfulness, non-harming, freedom from anger, compassion, gentleness, modesty. That's the Hindu test. Not what someone can do, but what they're like. Vrika had a power that could kill a god, and none of the list. A grandmother who is patient with everyone and never makes a show of her prayers may have the whole list and no powers at all. The tradition knows which one it bows to.
screen: `LET WHOEVER'S HEAD I TOUCH, DIE.` · `4.1: FIVE SOURCES OF POWER.` · `SELF-TORTURE IS ASURIC.` · `DAIVI SAMPAT: THE DIVINE QUALITIES.` · then, large: `POWER ISN'T HOLINESS; CHARACTER IS.`

segments.voice: Shiva has a name for being easy to please: Ashutosh. Vrika used it to bargain. Today, if you pray, say Om namah Shivaya a few times and ask for nothing at all. If you don't, bring to mind one person whose gentleness you trust, and rest there. Then pick one quality from the Gita's list, patience, gentleness, truthfulness, and carry it through the day.
Kaivalya, freedom, the name of the Yoga Sutras' fourth book. It opens by naming five sources of power, birth, herbs, mantra, discipline and samadhi, so that no power gets mistaken for freedom.
Your line: power isn't holiness; character is. Vrika had the power, and none of the divine qualities. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 480 COUNTS.` → `BOOK FOUR BEGINS.` → `TOMORROW: A KING OF HEAVEN BECOMES A SNAKE.`

howItsDone: Hindus honor tapas but judge holiness by character: teachers point to the Gita's divine qualities (16.1–3) and its warning against self-torturing, ego-driven austerity (17.5–6), and read Yoga Sutra 4.1 as a reminder that powers come from many sources.

Vrika.meaning: an asura who won a deadly boon from Shiva

Narada.meaning: a wandering sage who carries news between gods and people

Ashutosh.meaning: the easily pleased: a name of Shiva

tapas.meaning: the heat of discipline and austerity

asuras.meaning: powerful beings, often opposed to the gods

daivi sampat.meaning: the divine qualities: the Gita's measure of a holy person

Kaivalya.meaning: freedom; also the name of the Yoga Sutras' fourth book

samadhi.meaning: deep meditative absorption, the last of yoga's eight limbs

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.88 (Vrika asks Narada, wins his boon from Shiva by tapas at Kedara, and is undone by Vishnu as a young student)
Yoga Sutra 4.1 (powers born of birth, herbs, mantra, discipline or samadhi)
Bhagavad Gita 16.1–16.3 (the divine qualities) and 17.5–17.6 (terrible, self-torturing austerities of demonic resolve)

notes: Bhashya on 4.1: powers from birth (deha-antara, in another body) and herbs (rasayana in the abodes of the asuras): confirm.
The hummingbird is the script's illustration of 'birth', not from the commentary.
The reading of 4.1 as 'putting the powers in their place' is a common teaching reading; a Keeper may wish to name it as such.
